critiques.issue: The tree is empty. There are no Lvl1 claims, so nothing can be supported, refuted or prioritized, and any experiment run now is unguided search.
critiques.suggestion: Before the next run, write 3–4 Lvl1 hypotheses that split the objective into parts that can be measured separately. Suggested: H1 wall time is dominated by per-epoch throughput (data pipeline on 4 CPUs, precision, channels_last, torch.compile, kernel efficiency). H2 wall time is dominated by the number of epochs needed to reach 75%, i.e. sample efficiency (architecture width/depth, optimizer, LR schedule, label smoothing, EMA, augmentation strength). H3 fixed overhead in prepare/train is non-negligible (data loading to GPU, first-step compile or autotune leaking into timed regions). H4 the binding constraint is the accuracy margin, not speed: for a fixed recipe, time and margin trade off along a curve, and the recipe should sit just above 0.753 with variance accounted for. Each one needs at least one Lvl3 prediction with a numeric threshold.

critiques.issue: There are no experiments, not even the unmodified template baseline. There is no reference point for time or accuracy, and no estimate of run-to-run noise in either metric, so no future difference can be judged.
critiques.suggestion: Exp 1: run the unmodified submission_template as-is. Exp 2: repeat it exactly. The gap between them in `time`, and in per-seed accuracy if logged, sets the noise floor. Treat any later time improvement smaller than about 2× that gap as inconclusive (~) until it is replicated.

critiques.issue: The 0.753 gate on 3 fixed seeds is a weak proxy for the 40-seed ≥0.75 official judgment. CIFAR-100 short-schedule runs typically have a per-seed std of about 0.2–0.4%, so the 3-seed mean has an SE of about 0.15–0.25%. A run at 0.7535 is only about 1–2 SE above the official line. Because seeds 0/1/2 never change, tuning against them will also overfit to those seeds.
critiques.suggestion: Log per-seed accuracies and track the per-seed std. Mark any 'feasible' run with a mean below about 0.756 as fragile. Before claiming a final best, check it once with extra seeds if the harness allows it, or at least do not shave epochs right down to the 0.753 boundary on evidence from one run.

critiques.issue: Experiments run on an A100 SXM4 (400 W, higher sustained clocks and bandwidth), but judging uses an A100 PCIe (300 W). Recipes that are memory-bandwidth or power bound may rank differently there. Nothing in the tree accounts for this.
critiques.suggestion: Add a note or Lvl2 under H1: prefer improvements that reduce FLOPs or bytes moved over ones that only win on SXM-specific headroom. Do not read sub-percent time differences between close variants as meaningful for the official score.

critiques.issue: Several obvious speedups run into rules that nothing yet checks. torch.compile with dynamic batch sizes at eval can recompile, which can break the 5 s eval limit for B∈[1,1024]. Compile or autotune triggered by real data in prepare/train is timed. Caching anything derived from real data in build breaks the rules. Prepare must reset RNG, EMA and optimizer state. BN must stay frozen at eval.
critiques.suggestion: Add a standing compliance checklist experiment. Time eval at B=1, 7, 512 and 1024 after training. Assert that build never touches dataset files. Make sure compile/warmup in build uses synthetic tensors of every shape seen in train and eval, or mark dynamic dims explicitly, or run eval through an uncompiled path.

critiques.issue: Nothing from the known CIFAR speedrun literature is represented: airbench-style small ResNet/VGG, GPU-resident data with on-GPU flip/crop augmentation (very important with only 4 CPUs), BN-only weight-decay handling, label smoothing, Lookahead/EMA, whitening-initialized first conv, progressive resizing, and lower-resolution early epochs. Test-time flip augmentation is banned here, which removes one common airbench accuracy trick, so the epoch budget has to be larger than in CIFAR-10 references.
critiques.suggestion: Make 'move the entire dataset to GPU in prepare and augment on GPU' the first Lvl3 test under H1. Prediction: it cuts time by more than 30% versus a DataLoader baseline at equal accuracy (±0.3%). Put architecture/epoch-count sweeps under H2 only after the data pipeline stops being the bottleneck, or the two effects will be confounded.

critiques.issue: There are no preregistered predictions. Without a prereg written before each run, later verdicts can be fitted to the result after the fact.
critiques.suggestion: For every experiment, record the hypothesis id, the predicted direction and size of the effect on time and accuracy, and the noise threshold that separates + from ~, all before running. Give a single-run outcome at most a ~ or tentative +/- verdict until it is replicated.

structured_output.summary:
I have nothing to review yet: the hypothesis tree, the results table, the predictions table and the notebook are all empty. So no conclusion rests on a single run, and no hypothesis is contradicted yet, but every direction is still untried. The most important next steps are:
1. Run the unmodified baseline twice to measure noise in time and accuracy.
2. Write a Lvl1 tree that separates per-epoch throughput, epochs-to-target, fixed overhead and the size of the accuracy margin.
3. Preregister numeric predictions before each run.
4. Build a rule-compliance check for compile and eval timing.

Two structural risks need tracking from the start. First, the 3-fixed-seed 0.753 gate is only about 1–2 standard errors above the 40-seed 0.75 requirement, and tuning against the same seeds will overfit to them. Second, speed gains measured on the SXM card may not carry over to the PCIe judging card. The likely first win is GPU-resident data with augmentation done on the GPU, given only 4 CPU cores. Test it before any architecture or epoch tuning so the two effects aren't mixed up.
